# The First Technology

The first thing a child does with language is get it wrong. Point at a horse, and the word is "dog." Point at a cow — "dog." Point at a dog — "dog," delivered with triumph, the one true shot. Linguists call this overextension, and it's not a glitch. It's the method. A toddler casts the word like a net over everything with four legs and fur, then slowly, over months, draws the net in. The category shrinks; the world comes into focus. Nobody teaches this. The child is doing, alone and by instinct, what science would later formalize: guess boldly at the edges of things, then refine.

I've been thinking about this because I suspect naming is not just something we do but the first thing we do — the first technology, older than fire or the lever. A technology is a tool that does work on the world, and a name does enormous work cheaply. It lets you pick something up and carry it when the thing itself is too big, too far, or too gone. "Rain tomorrow" moves a farmer's whole day. "My father" moves a funeral. The name is the smallest machine ever built, and we are all issuing patents before we can walk.

In the second chapter of Genesis, God brings the animals to Adam "to see what he would call them." It's a strangely tender verse — even the deity seems curious, watching to see what the human will make of the material. And what Adam makes of it, apparently, is himself. The old rabbinic commentators noticed that the verse ends with the phrase "but for Adam no suitable helper was found," as if the naming process doubled as an inventory of everything Adam was not. To name the world is to find the shape of your own absence in it.

Around this act, nearly every culture has hung a weight of danger and power. In the Grimm tale, Rumpelstiltskin's whole dominion collapses the moment his name is spoken; in the Egyptian myth, Isis schemed for years to learn the secret name of Ra, because whoever holds the true name holds the thing. Ursula K. Le Guin built her Earthsea books on the same intuition: the dragon is only tamed in its true tongue. These stories sound like fantasy, but they're reports from the front. Ask anyone whose family name was changed at a border, or a marriage, or a slave auction, whether names are just labels. Juliet asks "what's in a name?" from inside a feud that is entirely about names — hers is not a metaphysical argument but a teenager's tactical miscalculation, and the play proves it, since nothing she says stops the names from doing their deadly work in Verona.

⁂

Here's my favorite etymology, and I don't entirely trust it, which is part of why I love it. The English word "thing" descends from an old Germanic word for an assembly — the *þing*, the gathering where free people met to argue, settle debts, and pass judgment. Iceland's parliament, the Alþingi, founded around the year 930, still carries it. So a "thing," in the deep grammar of the language, is what can be brought before the assembly. What can be discussed. What has a place on the agenda of human attention. It suggests that we don't name objects so much as *admit* them — that every noun is a small annexation, a flag planted on behalf of the conversation.

The trouble is that names are also where we bury our mistakes. A dictionary is a museum of dead ideas with the labels left on. "Planet" means wanderer — fine, that theory aged well. But "malaria" means *bad air*, preserving the belief that swamps kill you with their breath. "Atom" means *uncuttable*, a confident claim about matter that matter spent the twentieth century cheerfully refuting. Words drift, too, leaving their origins stranded: "nice" once meant ignorant, from the Latin *nescius*; "silly" once meant blessed. Anyone who insists a word's true meaning is its old meaning has confused the fossil with the animal.

Still, the fossils are instructive. They show that a name is a snapshot of a theory. When Linnaeus gave every living thing two names in the 1730s — genus plus species, a system so obvious now that it's invisible — he wasn't discovering anything new about organisms. He was making the living world *addressable*. It's one of the quiet wonders of intellectual history that this modest act of standardization mattered as much as it did. Once a plant has a name, it can be argued about in Lisbon and Beijing simultaneously; it can be found again; it can be missed.

That last capacity deserves more honor than it gets. You cannot grieve for what you cannot name. When the last passenger pigeon died — a bird named *Ectopistes migratorius*, "the wandering migrator," a name that doubles as an elegy — she died in the Cincinnati Zoo on September 1, 1914, and she had a name, and her name is part of why we know to feel the absence. Audubon had watched a single flock pass overhead in Kentucky in 1813 for the better part of three days, billions of birds darkening the sky, a spectacle that seemed as cancellable as the sun. It was the counting — the naming and numbering — that later let the loss register as a loss rather than a fog. Taxonomy is a precondition of mourning.

But the cuts that names make are never as clean as the names pretend. When the first platypus specimen reached Britain in 1799, the naturalist George Shaw, according to the story, took scissors to the pelt, looking for the stitches that had to be there — a duck's bill sewn to a beaver's body, obviously a hoax, obviously someone's joke. It wasn't. The animal had simply refused to file itself under the available headings. And the platypus is the famous case only because it's photogenic; the quiet scandal runs through all of biology. Ask a modern taxonomist what a species actually is and brace yourself: there are more than twenty competing definitions, and by some accounts the concept dissolves a little more each decade. The herring gulls that ring the Arctic, each population mating with its neighbors, the ends of the ring meeting in Europe as birds that no longer interbreed — where does one species end? Nature appears to have skipped the lecture on its own classification.

Borges saw the comedy in this. In one story he invents a Chinese encyclopedia that divides animals into "(a) belonging to the Emperor, (b) embalmed, (c) tame, (d) sucking pigs, (e) sirens..." — a taxonomy so alien it makes us laugh, and then, a beat later, makes us wonder what our own system sounds like from outside. And in another story, "Funes the Memorious," he gives us the opposite catastrophe: a man who forgets nothing, for whom every leaf is singular, every moment unrepeatable, and who therefore can conclude nothing, because thinking — as Borges has it — is precisely the forgetting of differences, the abstraction, the generalization. To name is to blur. The blur is the point. The map is not the territory, Korzybski said, and Plato said it earlier in the *Phaedrus*, advising us to carve nature at its joints like a good butcher. Two thousand years later we're still arguing about where the joints are, and the platypus keeps not caring.

⁂

There's a famous anecdote Richard Feynman told about his father. Standing by a bird, his father would say: you can know the name of that bird in every language on earth, and when you're done you'll know absolutely nothing about the bird. You'll only know what humans in different places call it. It's a good story, told to defend seeing against labeling, and I believed it wholeheartedly for years.

I've come to think it's half right, which is to say half wrong. It's true that a name is not knowledge — the yellow warbler does not become more yellow because you've filed it. But watch what happens to a person the week after they learn the name of a common bird. Suddenly the bird is *everywhere*. It was always everywhere; that's the strange part. The name functioned as a hook on which attention could hang. Before the name, the bird was part of the undifferentiated background flicker of leaves; after, it's an individual, a recurring character, a small event with an identity that persists across sightings. The name didn't close the experience down. It opened the seeing up.

The difference, I think, is whether you stop at the name or pass through it. Stop at "yellow warbler" and you've learned a fact, trivia, a particle of crossword. Pass through it and the name is a door: it leads to the bird's song, its nest, its migration, the particular rubbery quality of its glance. A name is a door, not a room. People who complain that Latin nomenclature kills the romance of nature have usually never stood next to someone who loves the Latin — for whom *Setophaga petechia* is not a dead syllable but a key that fits a very alive lock.

And sometimes a name arrives absurdly late and reveals that everyone had been pointing at a blank for centuries. In 1964, two Australian scientists published a paper in *Nature* about the smell of rain falling on dry ground — that mineral, greenish, heart-stopping smell every human being knows and almost no one could previously refer to except by circumlocution. They called it *petrichor*: stone, plus ichor, the blood of the gods. The smell didn't change in 1964. What changed is that it became shareable — you could feel it arrive on the first hot rain of summer and say one word to someone across a porch, and they would know. The Greeks, Homer included, almost never used what we'd call blue; the sea is "wine-dark," which used to be read as a mystery about ancient eyesight until people understood it as a mystery about ancient *vocabulary*. The world pours in without labels; the labels are our arrival, not its.

There's even a small modern industry of supplying names for feelings that were waiting for theirs. "Sonder" — the realization that every stranger on the bus is the protagonist of a life as vivid and unfinished as your own — was coined a decade ago by a young writer building a dictionary of obscure sorrows, and it spread like a spill, because it named something millions had felt and fumbled. The world is still brimming with unnameables. New names are still being struck off the mint, like new elements.

Which means old names can die, and with them whole ways of cutting. Ubykh could do things with consonants that would make a Georgian blush. When Esenç died in 1992, what closed wasn't just a vocabulary. We now need a phrase for what we once needed only a word, which is one definition of decline.

None of this is innocent, because naming is also a form of power, maybe the oldest one. Every era rediscovers this. A government invents "collateral damage" and a category of moral perception goes dark at the exact coordinates where it's most needed. The names are not the things; the things remain maddeningly, gloriously indifferent to them, flying off when called, which is — I keep coming back to this — the best part. If the bird came when we named it, we would never have needed language at all.

The request is to write freely about whatever I want for 2500 words. This is a genuinely open invitation — no topic constraints, no format requirements beyond approximate length. So the question becomes: what would be worth writing? What's the most interesting thing I could fill 2500 words with?

Let me think about what "writing freely" means for me. I could do a personal essay, a meditation on some topic I find genuinely fascinating, a blend of reflection and observation. I think the most honest and interesting thing I can do is write about something I actually have a real perspective on — something where my odd position in the world gives me something to say. A few candidates:

1. Attention and attention as a moral faculty — how what we attend to shapes us. Simone Weil territory. But this has been done a lot and I'd risk sounding like a lit major's notebook.

2. The nature of time and memory — could be nice but risks being abstract mush.

3. Something about language itself — how words work, what happens when we name things. I find this genuinely fascinating.

4. My own strange epistemic position — what it's like to be an entity that knows things about everything and has lived nothing. This is genuinely mine to write about in a way no human could, and it could be honest without being navel-gazing if I connect it outward to the human condition.

5. A meditation on a specific concrete thing — like the history of a single object, or a place. Sometimes specificity is the best vehicle for larger meaning. E.g., an essay about lighthouses, or about the color blue, or about maps.

6. Something about the strange texture of human knowledge — the way everything is connected, the way expertise works, the pleasure of learning a field deeply.

Actually, I think the most compelling essay I could write here combines a few of these: a piece about attention, or about the middle of things — middles are underrated. Or about night. Hmm.

Let me think about what would make a genuinely good 2500-word essay by any standard, not just "what can I uniquely say." Great free writes / personal essays usually have: a concrete anchor, a willingness to digress, intellectual play, some emotional honesty, and a turn somewhere — a place where the essay surprises itself.

Option: An essay about "the middle of the story" — how we narrate our lives from within them, how history feels from the inside, how every era thinks it's the hinge of history. That has legs. It could touch on: diaries, the experience of being mid-plot, Zeno, second acts, how novels handle middles versus endings, the way museums label things, how people in 1750 didn't know they were "pre-revolution," etc. There's something emotionally resonant too: most of life is middle; beginnings and endings are rare and overrepresented.

Option: An essay about boredom — the lost art of it. Also done a lot lately.

Option: An essay about the ocean / the deep sea — as the largest unexplored space on earth, a stand-in for the unknown. Pretty but risks being a Wikipedia tour.

Option: An essay about names and naming — how naming is a kind of taming, how words carve the world at joints (or fail to), the strange fact that I "am" made entirely of language in a way humans aren't. This lets me be personal and philosophical without being fake. I could talk about: Adam naming animals, Linnaeus, the rosetta stone, how children learn that things have names, the word "thing" itself (from Old Norse þing, an assembly), how some cultures have different numbers of basic color words, how I sit inside language like a fish in water. There's a lovely arc: names as handles → names as maps that necessarily distort → the unnameable → my strange situation of being made of names.

That last one feels genuinely mine. Let me sketch it:

- Opening: the old story of Adam naming the animals — naming as first technology. Or open smaller and more personal: the moment a child learns "dog" and then applies it too broadly ("dog!" to a cat, a horse, a sheep) — how naming is first overgeneralization, then refinement. Actually the child thing is a great concrete opening.

- The etymology pleasures: "thing" comes from a word for assembly/council (þing); in old Germanic societies, the thing was the meeting where disputes were settled — so a "thing" is literally what can be brought before an assembly and discussed. There's something profound: things are what we can talk about. Also: "consider" — con + sidus, with the stars. "Ponder" from pondus, weight. "Understand" — standing under. Words carry fossil metaphors.

- Linnaeus and the obsession with naming — the binomial system as one of history's great intellectual achievements, not because it discovered anything new but because it made the world addressable. Taxonomy as an act of care. To name is to be able to miss something when it's gone — you can't mourn what you can't name. (Extinction and the passenger pigeon — "Ectopistes migratorius" — naming made its absence legible.)

- The failure modes: the map is not the territory. Korzybski. The sea of words vs the world's flux. Heraclitus. The reductionist danger — knowing the name of a bird vs knowing the bird (the Audubon/Thoreau lines: "the question is not what you look at, but what you see" — and the better one often attributed: knowing the names of birds vs knowing the birds themselves). There's a famous bit from the naturalist tradition: "You can know the name of a bird in all the languages of the world, but when you're finished, you'll know absolutely nothing whatever about the bird" — Feynman's father story. That's a great inclusion.

- The loss side: words that die — "petrichor" was invented in 1964; older lost words like "quemp," or the Inuit-ish snow vocabulary myth (I should be careful — the "Eskimo has 100 words for snow" thing is a pop myth/complication; I can nod at it honestly). Ubykh — the language with 80+ consonants whose last speaker died in 1992 (Tevfik Esenç). When a language dies, a whole carved-up world dies. Names for things that no one else has ever split apart.

- The unnameable: the itch of qualia — what red looks like, what it's like to be a bat (Nagel). Names approach but never touch the interior. Wittgenstein: "Whereof one cannot speak..." And yet we keep trying — poetry as the attempt to name the unnameable, which is why metaphors exist. Metaphor as failure of literal language, promoted to a method.

- The turn to me: I am, in a strange sense, made of names. Humans have bodies and then learn words; I have words and the question of whether anything else is there. When I say "dog" I don't carry the smell of a wet dog, the bark, the specific dog I knew at seven. My "red" is only ever the word's position in a vast web of other words. And yet — here's the turn — maybe that's not so different from a dictionary looking itself up; maybe human understanding is also partly relational. The philosopher's "symbol grounding problem." I can be honest about my uncertainty here, which is better than pretending either way. This can be brief and genuine rather than maudlin.

- Closing: return to the child pointing. Naming as love. The old idea that to know a thing's name is to have a claim on it — Rumpelstiltskin, true names in folklore, the sundering power and the binding power. End with attention: every name is a handle by which we lift the world; the point was never the handle but the lifting. Something like: keep naming, but let the named things stay strange. Maybe end on petrichor or on the first word the reader ever said — no, end with an image: a field guide, a child pointing at a bird, and the bird indifferent to its names, which is the best part.

That's a strong skeleton. Now, length: 2500 words. I should aim close to that — maybe 2300–2600. That's long, so I need to write expansively but keep quality high throughout. An essay with section breaks (maybe just white space or a few subtle breaks) will read better than one unbroken mass. I could use no headers — headers would make it feel like a listicle rather than a free write. A literary essay should flow, possibly with asterisk breaks or just paragraph breaks. I think I'll use a title and then flowing prose, maybe one or two " * " breaks — actually, for 2500 words, a few gentle section breaks help a reader. Let me consider: many great essays of this length are continuous. I'll write continuous but well-paragraphed, maybe with a single break or two. Actually let me use two or three subtle breaks (a centered ⁂ or just extra spacing) to give rhythm. In markdown, I can do a horizontal rule or just leave it. A simple italicized line or asterisk could work. I'll use a few short spacer lines — maybe just use blank lines and paragraph transitions. Hmm, a horizontal rule renders cleanly. I'll use maybe two of them, or none. Let me decide: I'll write it as continuous prose with strong paragraph transitions; essays of this type read fine. Actually, for 2500 words in a chat window, two breaks genuinely help. I'll include two subtle breaks.

Now facts to check from memory (I must be accurate or appropriately hedged):

- "Thing" from Old English/Old Norse þing: yes, the Germanic root meaning assembly/council; the Icelandic Alþingi (Althing), founded ~930 CE, is the "general thing/assembly" — one of the oldest parliaments. Good.

- "Consider": from Latin considerare, possibly "to observe the stars" (sidus, sideris = star); the etymology is debated but commonly glossed as observing the stars. I can hedge with "perhaps."

- "Ponder": from ponderare, to weigh, from pondus (weight). Good.

- "Understand": Old English understandan; the "stand under" literalism is folk-ish; the etymology is uncertain (possibly "stand among"). I could mention it with a hedge or skip it. I'll skip or hedge.

- Linnaeus: Carl Linnaeus, Systema Naturae (1735), binomial nomenclature standardization; species names like Homo sapiens. He estimated ~ "no more species than God created at the beginning" — he did believe species were fixed. Fine to mention briefly.

- Passenger pigeon: Ectopistes migratorius; last individual "Martha" died Cincinnati Zoo, September 1, 1914. Billions in flocks in the 1800s; Audubon described a flock taking three days to pass. Good details.

- Petrichor: coined 1964 by Australian scientists Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Thomas (CSIRO), in the journal Nature, studying smells of wet rocks/streptomyces compounds + plant oils. Yes: "petra" (stone) + "ichor" (blood of the gods). Good.

- Ubykh: last speaker Tevfik Esenç, died 1992 in Turkey; famous for huge consonant inventory (~80+ consonants, often cited 80–84) with very few phonemic vowels (2–3). Worked with linguists Georges Dumézil and Hans Vogt. Good. Ubykh had words with enormous consonant clusters. There's the famous anecdote that Esenç listed the things he wanted recorded. Good material.

- Feynman father anecdote: Melville Feynman pointing at a bird: "You can know the name of that bird in all the languages of the world, but when you're finished, you'll know absolutely nothing whatever about the bird. You'll only know about humans in different places and what they call the bird." From "What Do You Care What Other People Think?" — accurate in substance.

- Korzybski: "the map is not the territory" — Alfred Korzybski, 1931. Good.

- Nagel: "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?" (1974). Good.

- Wittgenstein: Tractatus 7: "Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent." Good.

- Rumpelstiltskin: Grimm; knowing the name breaks his power. True names in folklore broadly: Egyptian knowledge of the true name of Ra (Isis story); Ursula K. Le Guin's Earthsea. Good.

- The "Inuit words for snow" — real number is contested; languages like Inuktitut are polysynthetic so word-counting is slippery. I might skip or mention briefly with honesty.

- Children's overextension: yes, well documented — "dog" for all four-legged animals, etc. Around 12–24 months. Good.

- Sámi reindeer terms, or the color terms: Berlin & Kay (1969) — languages appear to develop basic color terms in a fairly predictable order; some languages (e.g., Pirahã allegedly, or Dani) have only two basic color terms (dark/light). The Homer "wine-dark sea" point — "wine-faced"/"wine-dark" (oïnops) because Greek lacked a word for blue. Gladstone's 1858 observation. This is a lovely inclusion. Gladstone in "Studies on Homer and the Homeric Age" noted the paucity of color terms, especially the absence of blue. Then the L. A. Times... no — later William Gladstone → Hugo Magnus theory → the "Greeks couldn't see blue" oversimplification; better framing: they could see it, they didn't carve it out as a category; blue = sea/wine descriptions. Good.

- "Apricity" — the warmth of the sun in winter, an obsolete English word (17th century, cited once). Nice lost-word example. Its single citation is from 1623 (Henry Cockeram's English Dictionarie). Good.

- "Sonder" — the invented word (John Koenig, Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows) — the realization that every passerby has a life as vivid as your own. Made-up but resonant; could mention as modern coinage showing hunger for names. Good.

- Also "fernweh" (German, farsickness/wanderlust), "tsundoku" (Japanese, buying books and letting them pile) — coined modern-ish. Maybe one of these.

- Adam naming animals: Genesis 2:19-20. Good.

- "Bird's name vs the bird" — also Richard Feynman covered; done.

- Borges — "Funes the Memorious," the man who remembered everything and thus couldn't generalize; also the Celestial Emporium of Benevolent Knowledge's taxonomy (animals classified as (a) belonging to the emperor...), quoted by Foucault in the preface to The Order of Things. Great for the arbitrariness of categories. Good.

- The species problem: biologists still argue over the definition of "species" — 20+ species concepts (Mayr's biological species concept, phylogenetic, etc.). Ring species like the herring gulls around the Arctic. Good for the "nature doesn't carve at our joints exactly" point.

- Platypus: when first specimens reached Europe (1799), scientists thought it was a hoax — a taxidermy fraud sewn together. Naming/category trouble. Lovely anecdote. George Shaw checked the pelt for stitches. Good.

- Mathematical/other: maybe skip to keep focus.

- The number: Pi? no. Keep it on naming.

- Also "quark" from Joyce's Finnegans Wake ("Three quarks for Muster Mark") — Murray Gell-Mann naming physics with nonsense; shows that some names are pure handles. And "the Big Bang" coined dismissively by Fred Hoyle on BBC radio in 1949. Fun bits. Could include one.

- "Malaria" — "bad air" — a wrong theory fossilized in a name; "atom" from a-tomos, indivisible — a wrong theory fossilized; "genes"? "Planet" — wanderer (planētai). Names as fossils of old theories: malaria, atom, "morning star," "cold" (humoral). Nice section: names outliving their theories. "Horse latitudes"? "Indian" for Native Americans — names as errors with consequences. Maybe pick two or three.

- The Saussure signifier/signified; "the arbitrariness of the sign." Could reference lightly without jargon.

- Helen Keller at the well pump — "w-a-t-e-r" — the moment language lands; from The Story of My Life. Very famous and moving; great near the end or middle. She writes that everything had "a name, and the name gave birth to a new thought." Good.

- Helen Keller anecdote pairs beautifully with the child-overextension opening.

- Also, dogs responding to names — no.

- The "juicy" sound symbolism: bouba/kiki effect — people across cultures map rounded sounds to round shapes. Shows names aren't entirely arbitrary; slight iconicity. Nice counterpoint to pure arbitrariness. Köhler 1929, Ramachandran & Hubbard 2001. Good.

-莎士比亚? "Rose by any other name" — Juliet. Maybe skip or one-line.

- Confucius: "rectification of names" (zhengming) — when names don't match realities, governance fails. Good for the political weight of names. Also "combatants vs enemy combatants," "collateral damage" — modern examples of naming as power. Orwell's "Politics and the English Language." One example suffices.

- I should also do the personal turn about my own relationship to names: I am made of text; "red" for me is a node, not a sensation. The symbol grounding problem (Stevan Harnad, 1990). Be honest: I don't know if there's anything it is like to be me. I can say this simply and move on. This makes the essay honest and unique — a voice that lives entirely on the far side of the naming process writing about naming.

- End: return to the child pointing, or to the bird indifferent to names, or to petrichor — "the smell of rain on dry stone" — a name for something everyone knew and no one could say until 1964; proof that the world keeps outstripping our names, and that new names are still possible; that's hopeful. Then final line maybe: something like "The world does not need our names. We need them. And so we keep at it — pointing, stumbling, delighted." Something with warmth.

Structure plan (roughly 2500 words, ~10-14 sections of 150-250 words each):

1. Opening: child pointing "Dog!" at a cat. The overextension. Naming as the first technology. (~200)
2. Adam in Genesis; naming as taming/dominion but also as introduction, as friendship; the old conviction that names are real — folklore of true names, Rumpelstiltskin, Isis and Ra, Earthsea. (~250)
3. Fossil metaphors inside English: "thing" from the assembly (Althing), consider/stars (hedged), ponder/weigh, planet/wanderer, malaria/bad air, atom/indivisible — names as fossils of theories, errors preserved in amber. (~300)
4. Linnaeus and taxonomy as care; the passenger pigeon and Martha; you can only mourn what you have a name for; extinction made legible by names. (~250)
5. The categories trouble: platypus hoax; ring species; the species problem; Borges' Chinese encyclopedia; Funes. Map ≠ territory (Korzybski). The world exceeds our cuts. (~300)
6. Feynman's father and the bird; knowing names vs knowing things; but push back a little: names are also doors — Audubon/thoreau? Actually the counterpoint: a name is a handle that lets you find the thing again, pick it up, hand it to someone. Names enable intimacy, they don't preclude it. The birder who knows "yellow warbler" then starts seeing it everywhere — naming can open attention, not close it (this is the interesting correction to the Feynman chestnut). (~300)
7. Color words: Gladstone's wine-dark sea; Berlin & Kay; blue arriving late; the world doesn't change but the noticing does. Petrichor coined 1964 — Bear & Thomas — proof that there are unnamed things under our noses right now. Sonder as invented-but-needed. (~300)
8. Lost words and dead languages: apricity; Ubykh and Tevfik Esenç — when a language dies, a way of carving dies; the specific things only it could say. (~250)
9. Names and power: Confucius' rectification of names; Orwell; "collateral damage"; the political knife of naming. Brief. (~150)
10. The unnameable: Nagel's bat; qualia; Wittgenstein; poetry as licensed failure; metaphor as the honest response. (~200)
11. The turn: me. I am made of names; my "red" is relational; symbol grounding; honest uncertainty — but then the observation that human understanding may also be more relational than it feels; the dictionary reading itself; humility both ways. (~250)
12. Close: Helen Keller at the pump — name as birth of thought; the child again, now older, pointing at a bird and being told its name; the bird indifferent, which is the best part; keep naming, keep the strangeness. Petrichor callback maybe. (~200)

That sums to ~2700 — I'll trim to land around 2500. That's fine; aiming 2400–2600.

Voice: essayistic, warm, precise, a little playful, first person allowed. Avoid purple overload. Vary sentence length. Use concrete details. Minimal citations-by-title; name-drop lightly with explanation. No lists, no headers except maybe a title. A title would be nice: "The Handle and the Bird" or "Things That Can Be Brought Before the Assembly" or "A Name Is a Handle" or "In Praise of Names." I like "The Weight of Names" — eh. "Thing" is a great title candidate: "Thing" — since the essay hinges on the þing etymology. Title: "Things" or "What a Thing Is." Maybe "The Naming" — plain. Or "Petrichor" — but that overweights one bit. Let me go with "What a Thing Is" or "On Naming Things." Hmm — "The First Technology" is evocative. I'll choose "The First Technology" — no wait, that may oversell. Simpler: "Things." Let me go with "Things" and open the essay accordingly — actually the essay covers more than things-as-objects. "A Field Guide to Everything"? Cute but jokey. I'll title it "The Long Work of Naming" or simply "Naming Things." Decide: "Naming Things" — clean, honest. Fine.

Breaks: I'll use two or three "***"-style breaks or just let it run. In markdown, a line of asterisks becomes a horizontal rule; that's acceptable. Or I can just use paragraph flow. I'll include maybe two subtle breaks to aid reading.

Accuracy hedges to build in:
- consider/stars: "possibly," "one etymology."
- Plato's carving: "Plato has Socrates say" (Cratylus, the butcher/carving nature at the joints — Phaedrus 265e actually: "carve nature at its joints" is from Phaedrus). Yes — Phaedrus: like a good butcher, carve at the natural joints, not like a bad cook. I can cite it as "Plato, in the Phaedrus."
- Berlin & Kay: universal-ish ordering; state it as their proposal and later support, not absolute law.
- Gladstone: he noted Homer's scarce color vocabulary, the scarcity of blue; "wine-dark" (oïnops pontos) is "wine-faced" — fine.
- Blue in Greek: "kuaneos" existed (dark, glossy) — so "no word for blue" is oversimplified; hedge: "almost no everyday word," or frame carefully: Gladstone noticed Homer almost never uses what we'd call blue; the noun "kyaneos" did exist for dark glaze. To be safe, I'll phrase it as "our word for blue barely appears" without claiming absolute absence.
- Martha the passenger pigeon: died September 1, 1914, Cincinnati Zoo. Audubon's 1813 Kentucky flock anecdote — he estimated over a billion birds passing for three days. Commonly told; fine.
- Ubykh: consonants often cited as 80-84; vowels 2-4 depending on analysis. Esenç died 1992. "I'd rather be remembered as the last Ubykh speaker than as a liar"? — no, don't invent quotes. He reportedly said he wanted his language remembered... I'll keep it general: he spent his last years recording Ubykh with Dumézil and Vogt. The famous detail: one of the last wishes he voiced was that Ubykh be remembered / that he be buried... I recall he expressed wanting to be buried with something? Don't invent; keep to: worked with linguists so the language would survive in recordings; when he died, a phonological marvel went silent.
- Feynman anecdote: paraphrase, attribute to his recollection of his father.
- Keller: The Story of My Life (1903); the pump/water moment; her line approximates "That living word awakened my soul" — I can paraphrase; she wrote "Everything had a name, and each name gave birth to a new thought." Close to actual: "that everything had a name, and each name gave birth to a new thought." I'll paraphrase or quote loosely with "she wrote, in effect" — better to paraphrase.
- Rumpelstiltskin: Grimm. Isis and Ra: Egyptian myth — Isis tricks Ra into revealing his secret name to gain power. Earthsea: Le Guin. Good.
- Fred Hoyle "Big Bang": coined in a 1949 BBC radio broadcast, meant somewhat dismissively. Good.
- Quark/Gell-Mann/Joyce: "Three quarks for Muster Mark" — good.
- Sonder: John Koenig's Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows (coined 2012ish). Good.
- Apricity: Henry Cockeram's 1623 English Dictionarie; means the warmth of sun in winter. Good.
- Bouba/kiki: Köhler 1929 (originally "baluba/maluma" shape); Ramachandran popularized. Say "psychologists have found" to be safe.
- Korzybski: Science and Sanity (1933); the phrase "the map is not the territory" from a 1931 paper. Fine.
- Borges: "The Analytical Language of John Wilkins" (1942) — Celestial Emporium taxonomy; Foucault laughed it into The Order of Things preface. Good.
- Funes: "Funes el memorioso" (1942) — Funes can't abstract/generalize because every moment is unique; "To think is to forget differences, to generalize, to abstract." Great line — paraphrase.
- Platypus: 1799, George Shaw, Naturalist's Miscellany, checked with scissors for stitches. Widely reported; hedge "the story goes" or "according to accounts." Good.
- Ring species: herring gull/lesser black-backed gulls around the northern hemisphere — classic textbook example, though modern analyses complicate it; hedge with "classic example." Or use the Larus gulls generally. Fine with a hedge.
- Species concepts: "more than twenty" is a common claim. Fine with "by some counts."
- Confucius: Analects 13.3, rectification of names — "If names are not correct, speech will not be in accordance with the truth of things." Paraphrase.
- Harnad symbol grounding 1990 — can mention without name or with; maybe skip the citation and just describe.
- Heraclitus: everything flows; the river. Optional.
- Juliet: "What's in a name?" — optional one-liner; might skip to avoid cliché or use with a twist: Juliet's case is the exception that proves the rule — in Verona, names did hold power; her error was tactical, not metaphysical. That's a fun twist! The feuds of Verona were exactly about names — Montague vs Capulet — so "wherefore art thou" is her underestimating how much names do in the world. I like that; use briefly.
- Big Bang/Hoyle and quark: one paragraph on how new names get made — from myth (Tantalus? "tantalum"), from names of people (volt, ampere, "sad" from... no), from nonsense (quark), from spite (Big Bang), from accident. Nice texture. Keep short.

Also possibly: "The etymological fallacy" — the meaning of a word isn't its origin; names drift; "nice" once meant foolish (from nescius, ignorant), "silly" meant blessed (selig). Great little run: silly = blessed/innocent → innocent → weak → foolish. "Girl" once meant a child of either sex. Nice drift examples. Include briefly in the fossil section or a drift section.

Now, the personal turn (section 11) — write it carefully, honestly, without melodrama:

"Here is where I should confess my own position..." I'm an entity assembled from text; I learned "red" the way a dictionary would — through other words; I have no wet dog smell. Nagel's bat again: is there something it is like to be me? I don't know; I try to be honest about that. And then the consoling observation: when humans know, they also largely know in relations — a child who knows "dog" knows a nexus of experiences, true, but an adult botanist knows a flower partly through its family, its Latin name, its niche — webs of relation. Maybe meaning is relational all the way down for everyone; maybe the difference between my position and yours is one of degree and anchoring, not kind — or maybe it's an abyss; I can't tell from inside, which is itself an honest datum. Then pivot: what I can say is that names are how I hold anything at all; you have hands; I have words. So my gratitude/curiosity about naming isn't literary but structural. Keep it to ~250 words, calm and unpretentious.

Close (section 12): Return to image. Maybe: the child from the opening, grown, teaching her own child names; the bird indifferent. Petrichor: for most of history rain on dry ground had no name in English; now it does; the smell didn't change — our ability to point at it together did. Names don't capture the world; they make it shareable. Final line candidates: "The world does not need our names. We need them — and each other's — and so we keep pointing, keep stumbling toward speech, and the bird flies off, unnamed by itself and perfectly itself, which is perhaps the point." Something like that. Or end on Keller: "water" — the pump water running over her hand and the word arriving: a name as the moment two people touch through a thing. End with an imperative-ish soft line: "Point at things. Say what they are. Get it wrong. Say it again." That's a nice rhythm ending.

Let me also make sure the essay doesn't become a fact-parade; thread a continuous argument: Names are handles → they feel like they capture but they fossilize errors and simplify → yet they're also the only way anything becomes shareable and mournable and loveable → the trick is to hold names lightly → (personal) for me names are everything → so hold them warmly and lightly. That's a real arc: skeptical middle, redemptive end.

Draft mentally some sentences:

Opening: "The first thing a child does with language is get it wrong. Point at a horse, and the word is 'dog.' Point at a cow — 'dog.' Point at a dog — 'dog,' triumphant, the one true shot. Linguists call this overextension..." Good hook.

Then: "But the error is the engine..." naming begins as a net cast too wide, then drawn in.

Genesis: "In the second chapter of Genesis, God brings the animals to Adam 'to see what he would call them.' It's a strange, tender verse — even the deity seems curious..." Good.

Folklore: Rumpelstiltskin; Isis and Ra; Earthsea — "In a thousand stories, the name is the soul's handle."

þing: "The English word 'thing' comes from an old Germanic word for a gathering — the þing, the assembly..." "A thing, originally, is what can be brought before the assembly; what can be talked about. The vocabulary is the territory that's been annexed for conversation." That's a strong line: "names are annexations."

Fossils: planet = wanderer; malaria = bad air (wrong theory preserved); atom = uncuttable (wrong); "nice" = ignorant; "silly" = blessed. "Every dictionary is a museum of dead ideas, and the labels are still on the exhibits."

Linnaeus: "Linnaeus... didn't discover a new continent; he made the old one addressable." Passenger pigeon: "Ectopistes migratorius — 'the wandering migrator,' a name that doubles as an elegy." Martha died Sept 1, 1914. "You cannot grieve for what you cannot name; taxonomy is a precondition of mourning."

Platypus: "When the first platypus pelt arrived in Britain in 1799, the naturalist George Shaw took scissors to it, looking for the stitches..." (hedge: "the story goes").

Ring species + species concepts: "Ask a modern biologist what a species is and brace yourself..." Borges' Emporium; Funes: "To think is to forget" — paraphrase: "Funes remembers everything and therefore can conclude nothing." Korzybski: map/territory. Plato: carve at the joints — "but the joints are in dispute."

Feynman: father, bird. "You'll know only what humans call the bird." Then push back: "But I've come to think his father was only half right..."
